learningObjective: Apply the α + βS communication cost model to distinguish latency-dominated from bandwidth-dominated regimes for small vs large collectives.

canonicalClaims.claim: The point-to-point cost model T(S) = α + β·S has a latency-dominated regime (α ≫ β·S) for small S and a bandwidth-dominated regime (β·S ≫ α) for large S; the crossover payload is roughly S* = α / β.
conditions: α (fixed launch/latency per message) and β (inverse bandwidth) are non-negative constants for the link.
The message is a single non-pipelined transfer between two endpoints; collectives compose multiple such terms.
nonImplications: Does not imply that time is linear in S in the latency regime; the linear component is dominated by α there.
Does not imply that AllReduce has the same α and β as point-to-point; algorithm-specific factors (like 2(N-1)/N) apply.

sourceMappings.locator: Ch. 6 communication cost decomposition into latency and bandwidth
§3 cost model used by the partitioner

misconceptions.claim: For any two payload sizes S1 and S2 with S1 < S2, the cost ratio is exactly S1/S2 because the model is linear.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The model α + β·S is affine, not proportional; when α dominates, doubling S barely changes T. The ratio S1/S2 only holds when α ≪ β·S on both sides.

misconceptions.claim: The latency term α can be ignored on modern high-bandwidth interconnects (NVLink, InfiniBand), so the model reduces to T = β·S.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Small-message α (kernel launch, NIC handshake, driver overhead) remains in the microsecond range even on fast fabrics, dominating below ~100 KB payloads for many stacks.

misconceptions.claim: The crossover S* = α / β is a hardware constant that doesn't depend on the collective algorithm.
misconceptions.whyWrong: α and β for a collective depend on the algorithm (ring, tree, halving/doubling), on the number of ranks, and on the software stack — S* varies accordingly.
